title: Why Raised-Root Trip Hazards Are Worth Fixing Before Snow Cover
meta_title: Raised-Root Trip Hazards Before Snow Cover
meta_description: A raised root that's visible now becomes a hidden hazard once snow covers the yard. Here's why late fall is a good time to have it addressed.
lede: A raised root you can see and step around right now becomes a very different problem once snow is covering the ground.
excerpt: Why late fall, before snow cover, is a good time to deal with raised-root trip hazards.

sections.heading: Visibility Changes Everything About the Risk
paragraphs: A raised root sitting in the open is something people naturally learn to step around. Once snow covers the yard, that same root becomes invisible, and the trip risk goes up substantially for anyone crossing that part of the property.

sections.heading: Root Removal Is Part of a Stump Grinding Job
paragraphs: Raised roots can be removed as part of a stump grinding job, which makes late fall, before snow arrives, a practical time to have them addressed alongside any stump that's already on the list.

sections.heading: Who's Most at Risk
paragraphs: This matters most in yards with regular foot traffic through winter, driveways, walkways, and paths to outbuildings, where a hidden root under snow is far more likely to actually be stepped on.

sections.heading: The Window Is Closing With the Season
paragraphs: Root removal works the same way stump grinding does when it comes to timing: it's more straightforward while the ground is still workable, which means addressing it before the first snow, not after.

faqs.q: Are raised roots more dangerous once it snows?
faqs.a: Yes, snow cover hides them, which significantly increases the trip-hazard risk compared to when they're visible.

faqs.q: Can raised roots be removed without a full stump grinding job?
faqs.a: Root removal is typically handled as part of a stump grinding job, so it's most practical to address alongside any stump work already planned.

faqs.q: Where does this matter most on a property?
faqs.a: Areas with regular winter foot traffic, like driveways, walkways, and paths to outbuildings, are where a hidden root is most likely to actually cause a fall.
